---
title: "Where you are now"
---

Your first program was one line. You typed `circle(200, 260, 360);`
into a playground in your browser, pressed Run, and a circle appeared.
The same chapter showed you the line with a capital C, which draws
nothing, and that was the lesson every other chapter has quietly relied
on since: the computer takes you literally. Your last program was a
slot machine with a picture sheet, a spinning animation, credits, and a
check that passes, written in a folder of your own with nothing prepared
for you.
This short chapter is the pause between those two programs and whatever
you build next.

## What you carry out of this book {#sec-what-you-have}

Look at the chapter list once more, from the top. Every part added one
idea, and each idea only made sense because the one before it was
already yours.

- **Values with a name.** A variable is a box with a name and a type,
  and a program is a story of values moving between boxes.
- **Decisions.** An if statement asks a question and runs one branch or
  the other. A switch asks the same question six times at once.
- **Repetition.** A loop lets you say "again" without typing it again,
  and a loop inside a loop gave you grids, meshes, and chessboards.
- **Many values under one name.** An array holds a whole row, and you
  know the difference between copying a number and copying the arrow
  to an array, which many people who program for a living never quite
  learned.
- **Commands of your own.** A function takes parameters, may answer
  with a return value, and can even be handed to somebody else to call
  later.
- **A workshop of your own.** VS Code, Node.js, npm, and Biome. You can
  unpack a project, install its packages, format it, check it, and run
  it without a playground preparing any of it for you.

None of these are toy versions. `let`, `if`, `for`, arrays, functions,
and `npm install` are the same words a professional types on a Monday
morning. The programs were small so that you could see every part of
them, and that is the only difference.

## Two habits that matter more than any command {#sec-habits}

The command list above is easy to look up again. Two things from this
book are harder to find in a reference, and they are the ones you should
keep.

The first is **pen and paper before the keyboard**. You played computer
with a table of `mouseX` values, you drew a silo with its constants
labeled before you drew it in code, and you predicted what
`console.log` would print before you ran it. Every time your prediction
was wrong, you learned something the running program alone would have
hidden. Keep doing that. A sketch on paper is the cheapest debugging
tool you'll ever own.

The second is **only what you can explain**. You may look anything up,
and you may ask an AI for help, and that stays true next year and in
every job after it. The rule is that whatever ends up in your file, you
can walk through line by line and say why it's there. Code you can
explain is yours. Code you can't explain is borrowed, and borrowed
code fails you at the worst moment, usually in an exam or in front of a
customer.

## Keep making things {#sec-keep-going}

The folder on your computer doesn't go away when the course ends, and
neither does what you know. Until the next part of this course starts,
make something. It doesn't have to be big, and it doesn't have to be
good. Take the bouncing ball and give it gravity. Give the slot machine
a sound, or a second player. Draw the flag of a country you'd like to
visit, with a loop for the stripes. Redo Word Swirrel with a word that
means something to you. The point isn't the result; the point is that
you open VS Code without anyone telling you to, and that your fingers
remember `npm start`.

When something breaks, and it will, read the error message from the
beginning, the way you learned in the very first part. Then sketch.
Then ask. That order has not changed since your first circle, and it
won't change next year either.

## What comes next {#sec-next-book}

This book drew on a canvas. The next book, *Creative Coding 2*, keeps
the language and the tools you have now and changes the world they
work in. Instead of painting pixels, your program builds a web page out
of elements, styles them with CSS, draws with SVG, and reacts to clicks
and keystrokes on that page. A web page turns out to be full of
**objects**, things that have properties and can do things, and by
working with the page's objects you learn what an object is. Later you
write your own, with classes, and you test them so that you can prove
they work instead of hoping. Every one of those chapters stands on a
variable, a loop, an array, and a function, so you already have the
ground it's built on.

That is the whole plan. You came in with no programming experience, and
you leave with a workshop, a slot machine, and the habit of predicting
before you run. Close the laptop, take a walk, and be a little proud of
that. See you in the next book.
